tagline.text: A eucalyptus-shaded park and football stadium in Bacolod, home of Negros's biggest festival

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (transport and meals; admission and event fees extra)

children.text: Panaad Park is a roughly 25-hectare sports and recreation park run by the Negros Occidental provincial government, with Panaad Stadium, swimming pools and a eucalyptus grove. It is also the permanent home of the annual Panaad sa Negros Festival.

Panaad Park is a sports and recreation park in Barangay Mansilingan, south of Bacolod. It covers roughly 25 hectares and is planted with about 60,000 eucalyptus trees. The Negros Occidental provincial government owns and manages it, and it is also called Panaad Sports and Recreation Park or Panaad Park and Stadium. "Panaad" is a Hiligaynon word meaning a vow or promise.

The park began with the 1998 Palarong Pambansa, the national schools games. The stadium and sports complex were built to host it and were first called the Negros Occidental Sports and Recreation Center. Construction ran from August 1997 to April 1998, and the Centennial Palarong Pambansa was held there right after. When the Panaad Festival later settled here, the whole park became known as a festival ground.

The heart of the park is Panaad Stadium. It has a natural-grass football pitch and an athletics track, and it has hosted international events such as the football tournament of the 2005 Southeast Asian Games and the 1999 AFC Women's Championship. Ceres–Negros FC used it as their home ground from 2015 to 2020, and it also staged AFC Cup and Philippines Football League matches. Wikipedia says the stadium closed for renovation in January 2020 and reopened in March 2023, though the same article gives both March 21 and March 30 as the date. Please check whether it is open before you visit.

For travelers, the main attraction is the row of 32 pavilions in the park. Each city and town of Negros Occidental takes one and presents its history, local products, tourist spots and food. The pavilions are liveliest during the festival; outside it the park feels more like a quiet sports ground. It is best treated as a place to visit on a schedule. Two approaches work well for first-timers: go during the festival for the pavilions and shows, or walk the grove on a weekday morning and combine it with the rest of your Bacolod day. Either way, plan only half a day here and fill the rest with the cathedral, markets and inasal restaurants in town. This is a local exercise park and event ground rather than a polished tourist attraction, and knowing that narrows the gap between expectation and reality.

Known as the "festival of festivals" of Negros Occidental. It started in 1993 at the Capitol Park and Lagoon, moved to the area near Bredco Port in 1997, and now has this park as its permanent venue. Expect an opening Mass, pavilion openings, the Lin-ay sang Negros pageant and a festival dance competition.

Each of the 32 local governments of Negros Occidental decorates its own pavilion. You can sample local products, handicrafts and food from across the province in one place, like a fair that condenses the whole province. The pavilions may be closed outside festival time.

. It has hosted Philippine national team and AFC Cup matches, and a record crowd of about 20,000 reportedly attended the match against Mongolia in 2011. Catching a match-day atmosphere is a good reason to visit.

About 60,000 eucalyptus trees stand throughout the park, so there is plenty of shade even at midday. The air feels cool despite the park being close to the city, which suits a morning walk or jog. Many local families spread out mats and relax here.

The park has the Panaad Swimming Complex, with an Olympic-size pool and a training pool. We found no published information on public opening hours or fees, so confirm on site. Access may be restricted on days of competitions or training.

Besides football, the stadium is used for concerts and local sports competitions. Follow announcements from the provincial government and organizers for schedules, and expect crowded roads nearby on big event days.

Bacolod has the October MassKara Festival, while Panaad is a province-wide festival held in spring. MassKara heats up the city streets with masks and dance, whereas Panaad centers on local-government exhibits and cultural events, so the two feel different. Experiencing both gives a broad understanding of Negros culture.
Take a jeepney from downtown Bacolod to the park. During the festival, go early to avoid the crowds.
Check the day's program near the entrance and start walking through the pavilion area.
Pick the local-government pavilions you are interested in and browse their products and handicrafts. Try a small taste if there is a sampling corner.
Have lunch at a food stall in the park or a restaurant nearby.
Rest along the shaded eucalyptus paths, then watch an afternoon event or performance.
Head back to the city by jeepney or Grab before sunset.
Festival schedules change every year, so check the provincial government and the official festival announcements before you go.

items.title: Weekday Walk
items.subtitle: Grove paths and the stadium exterior

children.text: Arrive early in the morning and walk the eucalyptus paths. Local joggers are out, which gives a good feel for the place.
Walk around the outside of the stadium and look at the exterior and the area around the track. Ask on site whether the inside is open.
Snack at a shaded rest area, then return to the city and continue to The Ruins or the Capitol Park.

On weekdays the pavilions are likely to be closed, so this route is for walking and viewing the exterior. If you want to go inside the stadium, ask the provincial sports office or the park management beforehand.
Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific and AirAsia fly from Manila to Bacolod-Silay Airport (BCD). Schedules vary by season and airline, so check before booking.
The airport is in Silay, north of Bacolod, not in the city itself, so you need a separate transfer into town.

The best time to enjoy Panaad Park is during the Panaad sa Negros Festival. It ran April 15–21 in 2024 and March 24–30 in 2025, so the dates change every year. There is no fixed schedule, so check the provincial government's announcements before you visit.
Outside the festival, the November–May dry season is best for walking. Midday sun is strong, so mornings or late afternoons are better. In the rainy season frequent showers limit outdoor activity.

If you want to see a match, check the Philippines Football League or international fixtures separately. Evening matches under the floodlights have a great atmosphere, but after the final whistle jeepneys and Grab are in heavy demand and you may wait a long time.

items.note: Two travel guides say the park has no regular entrance fee, but this is not officially confirmed. Events such as the Panaad sa Negros Festival, or specific facilities, may charge separately.

There is no lodging inside the park; hotels are clustered in Bacolod city. Mid-range options listed include O Hotel and Northwest Inn, while upscale ones include Planta Hotel & Residences and Park Inn by Radisson. Prices vary by season and room, so check on a booking site. During the festival rooms fill quickly, so book early.
Be sure to try inasal (grilled chicken), Bacolod's pride. At inasal streets such as Manokan Country it is listed at about
. For snacks, piaya, kalamay hati, napoleones and pinasugbo are well known. During the festival you can also taste regional specialties at food stalls near the pavilions.
There is no large shopping mall close to the park, so it is wise to buy water and snacks in town beforehand. You can have lunch back in the city, or at a stall inside the park during the festival.
Festival dates change every year, so check Panaad's official announcements and provincial government news first.
Even with plenty of shade, the midday sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
When boarding a jeepney, check for the "Alijis" or "Mansilingan" sign and tell the driver where you are getting off.
On match or concert days the roads clog up, so allow plenty of time for the trip back.
Wear comfortable walking shoes. The park is large and you will walk more than you expect.
Carry some cash. Street stalls and jeepneys often do not accept cards.
The stadium interior and the swimming pool may close depending on the event schedule, so inquire before you go.
The festival is good for photographing the pavilions, but in crowded spots keep your belongings in front of you.
It is easy to get lost inside the park, so save the entrance and stadium locations in your map app first.
The park is quiet on ordinary days and event schedules change often. Always confirm whether the stadium and pavilions are open, and the admission fee, before you go.
The stadium is reported to have closed for renovation from January 2020 and reopened in March 2023. Check the latest announcements for what is currently open.

We found no confirmed official source for opening hours (guides say typically early morning to evening, but the stadium may differ), and only guides, not official sources, say there is no regular admission fee. Asking on site or the provincial government is the most reliable way.
During the festival, watch for pickpockets and crowds, and keep valuables close to your body.
On very hot days do not overexert yourself; rest often in the shade.
Some sources place the park in Alangilan, but most say Mansilingan, so confirm the location in a map app.

blocks.title: Negros Occidental Provincial Capitol and Lagoon

children.text: The place where the Panaad Festival was first held, about
20 minutes
from downtown by car. Festival opening events are sometimes held here.
A mask festival that fires up downtown Bacolod in October. Seeing it alongside Panaad is a good way to compare Negros festival culture.
The ruins of an old mansion on the edge of Talisay, a good place to combine with Bacolod in a day.
A base for seeing downtown Bacolod's churches, inasal street and markets together.
